inline_comments.comment: `component` is typed as `ComponentRef | undefined` (returned by `findMatchingComponent`), but starting here it is accessed without a null check: `component.reactDocgen`, `component.reactDocgenTypescript`, `component.reactDocgenTypescriptError`, and `component.path`. The guard above (`if (!experimentalReactComponentMeta && !hasDocgen)`) only returns early when `experimentalReactComponentMeta` is false — so when the flag is enabled and no component is found (e.g. story JSX analysis yields no matches), every one of these accesses throws a TypeError at runtime. The fix is to add an unconditional null guard (`if (!component) { return { manifest: { ...base, error: ... } }; }`) before reaching this block, identical to what already exists for the docgen path.

`debug: componentMetaDebug` is added to the returned `meta` object, but `ComponentsManifest.meta` in `core-common.ts` declares no `debug` field. This is an undeclared field that TypeScript may not catch due to structural typing in the preset call chain, but it leaks debug data into a public manifest shape, breaks the type contract for any consumer that reads `ComponentsManifest.meta`, and may be serialised into the JSON response served to browsers. Either add `debug?: Record<string, unknown>` to the type declaration, or log the data via `logger.debug` instead of embedding it in the manifest.

Disabling `@typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars` for this entire override block is broader than necessary. The actual intent is to silence `_props`-prefixed parameters in test fixtures — but the `_` prefix convention (already used throughout those fixtures) is exactly what the rule is designed to respect. Keeping the rule enabled and relying on the `_` prefix is cleaner. A global off here would hide real unused-variable bugs in any TypeScript file that falls under this override.

`fs.watch` with `{ recursive: true }` was not supported on Linux until Node.js 20 (via inotify). On earlier runtimes the call throws immediately; the surrounding `try/catch` silently swallows it and logs a `debug`-level message, so file watching silently stops working with no user-visible warning. Storybook targets a broad range of Node versions. Consider emitting a `logger.warn` when the watcher fails, or documenting the minimum Node version required for incremental prop updates to work.

`extractDefaultsFromSourceFile` calls `typescript.sys.readFile` and `typescript.createSourceFile` on every invocation with no caching. It is called from `serializeComponentDocs` for every component whose source resolves to a `.d.ts` file, which is common in monorepo/package-import setups. For a design system with hundreds of components this means hundreds of synchronous file reads and full AST parses per manifest pass. A simple `Map<string, Map<string, string>>` keyed by `(filePath, exportName)` would eliminate the redundant work.

The `catch` block here silently drops all extraction errors with only a brief comment. When a component fails to extract (e.g. due to a TypeScript internal error, a bad type, or an unexpected AST shape), there is no observable signal. A `logger.debug('[reactComponentMeta] Failed to extract props for ...', err)` line would make the failure diagnosable without breaking the batch-extraction guarantee.

`docgenTimings` is module-level mutable state that is mutated inside `getComponents` and reset by `resetDocgenTimings`. In a test environment where tests run in the same process, parallel or interleaved test executions can corrupt each other's timing data, producing unreliable metrics. Consider passing the timings object as a parameter to `getComponents`, or accumulating timings locally inside `manifests` and returning them rather than using a shared module-level accumulator.

Five substantial test cases (DtsComponent, ForwardRef, RenamedExport, DisplayNameOverride, Barrel) are deleted with only a brief comment. These tests documented *why* RDT fails on those patterns — which is the primary motivation for the new engine. Replacing them with `it.skip(...)` annotated with the failure reason would preserve the intent as regression documentation and make it clear that these patterns are expected to fail in RDT, rather than looking like coverage was simply dropped.

`process.once(signal, ...)` is called inside `getManager`, which is invoked once per manifest pass (but cached via `managerPromise`). If the module is re-evaluated during development (e.g., a hot-reload that re-runs the preset), `managerPromise` resets to `undefined`, a new manager is created, and new signal handlers are registered — while the old manager's file watchers and TS programs are never disposed (the old `process.once` handlers still hold a closure reference but won't fire until the signal arrives). Over multiple reloads this accumulates open file descriptors and TS programs. Consider disposing the previous manager explicitly when `getManager` detects an already-existing (but stale) instance, or expose a `resetManager()` for use in tests and hot-reload scenarios.

`--max_old_space_size` for the UI build was silently increased from 4096 to 5120 MB with no accompanying comment explaining why. A comment explaining what changed (e.g. "Increased due to additional TS LanguageService memory usage from react-component-meta") would make this easier to review and track.

general_comments.comment: The null-dereference issue with `component` (detailed in the inline comment at generator.ts ~line 272) has a cascading effect: `component.path`, `component.reactDocgenTypescriptError`, and `component.member` are all accessed without optional chaining after the partially-guarded `hasDocgen` check. It is worth doing a single pass to add a unified null guard at the top of the non-error branch so that every subsequent access to `component` is safe, rather than retrofitting individual optional chains.

The `timings.reactComponentMetaComponents` field is a count of components processed rather than a duration, yet it is embedded in the `timings` object alongside millisecond values. Naming (`*Ms` suffix for durations vs. `*Count` for counts) or structure (separate `counts` sub-object) would avoid ambiguity for tooling or dashboards that consume the manifest `meta`.
